UNDERWATER AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS / PATH PLANNING / ROS 2

MANTA: avoidance decisions and path planning for an underwater vehicle

I built the avoidance-decision and path-planning modules that let an underwater vehicle evade an approaching torpedo while following its mission path. I applied A* and Dynamic VO (DVO) separately and checked path following and avoidance results in Gazebo.

Period
2026.07–2026.08
Project
Team project, LIG D&A The SSEN Embedded Software School
My role
Avoidance decisions, path planning, experiment design and automation
Stack
C++17, ROS 2, Gazebo, Python
MANTA GitHub ↗

Evasive motion against an approaching threat

Show planned-path visualization
01 / SYSTEM

My part of the system: avoidance decisions and path generation

The module takes BlueROV2 and threat states, decides whether to evade, and passes the path from the selected planner to the control module. I was responsible for the avoidance decision, path generation, interface integration and experiment automation.

To focus on validating the decision and planning logic, BlueROV2 and torpedo positions came from the Gazebo simulation.

02 / APPROACH

A* routes around risk zones; DVO compares motion candidates

I implemented two approaches to see how the avoidance method changes the outcome against a moving threat. A* builds a global path around the predicted risk zone. DVO accounts for relative motion and re-selects a local avoidance direction at every step.

A* / GLOBAL PATH

Path to the goal around the risk zone

The torpedo’s expected travel area is added as an obstacle, and A* searches for a path to the mission goal that avoids it. A valid path is kept. If the goal changes or a collision becomes possible, the path is replanned.

DVO / LOCAL PATH

Local avoidance path from compared candidates

Using the threat’s current position and estimated velocity, DVO compares the expected closest distance to the threat for each motion candidate. Candidates are re-evaluated with every new state to produce a short-range avoidance path.

Show algorithm settings

A* risk zone

Obstacles are the current 3×3×3 m box plus boxes at positions predicted from the guidance behavior. The prediction horizon is 4.0 s, boxes are spaced about 1.5 m apart, and up to 32 future boxes are used. Each value is a separate limit, not a fixed corridor length.

DVO candidate evaluation

Relative motion is evaluated over 6.0 s, assuming the current torpedo box moves at its estimated velocity. There are up to about 1,263 velocity candidates, limited to 3.0 m/s horizontally and ±1.5 m/s vertically. The planning clearance of about 3.85 m is the sum of the vehicle radius, the box circumscribed radius and a margin, and differs from the 1.0 m hit criterion.

03 / IMPLEMENTATION

Fixing a vehicle that stopped even when a path existed

Instead of building the full path to the mission goal at once, DVO repeatedly generates a short avoidance path from the current state. Connecting it to the existing path-following module exposed two problems.

Accepting short avoidance paths

Problem
A short, drivable partial path did not meet the existing hand-off condition, so it never reached the control module.
Fix
I changed the condition so short drivable partial paths are also passed on, letting the control module receive the next path and keep moving.

Separating the path end from the mission goal

Problem
Reaching the end of a short avoidance path was treated as the end of the whole mission.
Fix
I separated the local path end from the final mission goal so the vehicle receives and follows the next path.

I separated the decision and planning logic from the ROS runtime code so it could be tested on its own. I automated runs for each experiment condition and CSV log collection, so every result was checked against the same criteria.

Show code structure

Decision logic in isolation

PlanningCore decides whether to evade, and at what velocity, from the latest vehicle and threat states. ROS I/O and planner execution are kept separate so the decision logic can be tested independently.

Connection to path following

Partial paths with two or more points are passed to the control module, and the local end point is kept. When the same goal is received again, only its timestamp is refreshed, so the path and control state are not reset unnecessarily.

Rates and visualization

Path-planning requests run at 5 Hz and control at 20 Hz. Pending inputs are replaced with the latest state. Grouping the initial box markers into a CUBE_LIST cut visualization traffic from 165 msg/s to 5 msg/s.

Experiment automation and checks

Everything from condition setup to execution, collection of six CSV log types and the final verdict is automated. Only batches that passed a log-integrity check went into the results, and 14 ROS/C++ Debug regression tests passed.

04 / VALIDATION

Avoidance results changed with the threat conditions

I implemented and tested both A* and DVO. The results below summarize DVO across 24 conditions as the representative result.

Direct pursuit (SimpleTracking) steers toward the target’s current direction. Proportional navigation (PN) adjusts the approach direction using the relative motion between torpedo and target.

I tested 24 conditions: four approach directions (head-on, rear, side, diagonal), two guidance laws and three torpedo models.

A run counted as an evasion only if the vehicle was not hit before the torpedo ran out of fuel. Because the torpedo can turn and attack again after a miss, evading only the first approach did not count as a final evasion.

With one final run per condition, DVO achieved final evasion in 15 of 24 conditions.

DVO final evasion results; each cell is the number of conditions evaded out of three torpedo models

Final evasion succeeded in 11 of 12 direct-pursuit conditions and 4 of 12 proportional-navigation (PN) conditions.

With the same DVO planner, the result depended heavily on the torpedo’s guidance law.

Trajectory for a representative condition

Trajectories are shown in the horizontal plane. A hit was defined as a 3D distance of 1.0 m or less between the two vehicles.

Show closest distances and planning times

There was no A* control group on the same latest code, so I did not rank the two planners quantitatively.

For completed planning calls, the median time was 1.243 ms and the p95 was 2.921 ms. The median number of planning calls per run was 412.5.

I connected the avoidance decision and path planning to the control module and checked the vehicle’s behavior and final result in each condition. Separating the effects of DVO’s constant-velocity prediction and the simulated vehicle’s acceleration and turning response on avoidance remains open work.
